passage:
Class 3B observation note, written by Darshan, class teacher.
Chaitanya stood beside my desk at every break this week, asking, "Sir, you're not angry with me, na?" Four or five times a day. Some colleagues call it a bid for attention. I don't think so; he looks tense until I answer.
What I did: I told him warmly each time that I'm not angry. Then I gave him a small job: taking the attendance register to the office alone and coming back to tell me. On Monday he ran both ways. By Friday he walked, and stopped to chat with Irfan on the stairs.
Next step: one break a day at the swings, with me waving from the window.

qa.q: What job did the teacher give Chaitanya?
qa.a: Taking the attendance register to the office alone and coming back to tell him.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's question "you're not angry with me, na?" suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He seems anxious and needs to be sure his teacher is still on his side; he looks tense until he gets an answer.

qa.q: What choice did Darshan make instead of treating it as a bid for attention, and why did it work?
qa.a: He answered warmly each time and added a small solo job, so Chaitanya felt safe and slowly grew braver.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the trip to the office by Friday?
qa.a: It likely feels less scary and more his own, since he walks calmly and stops to chat with Irfan.

grounding: A teacher notices a boy who shadows him and needs repeated reassurance, and responds with steady warmth and small steps toward independence.

passage: 14 March. Asif followed me round the school library again today like a small shadow, holding a book he wasn't reading. "Arnab sir, are you staying here the whole period?" Three times he asked. The PT teacher laughed and said the boy just wants attention. Maybe. But his shoulders dropped each time I said yes. So I said yes, kindly, every time. Then I asked him to shelve the red-spine books in the far corner and come show me when he'd done five. He looked back twice, but he did it. Tomorrow, ten books. Small steps. Note to self: ask his mother how mornings go at home.

qa.q: Which books did Arnab ask Asif to shelve?
qa.a: The red-spine books in the far corner.

qa.q: How can you tell that Asif was anxious rather than just seeking attention?
qa.a: He kept asking if Arnab would stay, and his shoulders dropped with relief each time he heard yes.

qa.q: What small independence step did Arnab choose, and why does it suit Asif?
qa.a: He asked Asif to shelve five books in the far corner and come back, a short, safe distance that can grow to ten tomorrow.

qa.q: How does the PT teacher see Asif differently from Arnab?
qa.a: The PT teacher sees a boy wanting attention, while Arnab notices the relief in Asif's shoulders and answers with warmth.

grounding: A teacher's diary shows a boy who shadows him and needs reassurance, met with steady warmth and a small step toward independence.
